newsitem.title: DUBAI: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - hugging five-year highs.
newsitem.headline: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - hugging five-year highs.

text.p: Gulf gas oil is expected to be highly sought after in the coming week, in contrast to jet kerosene which is struggling to move at current high prices for refined products, Gulf traders said on Thursday.
Gas oil rose to $28.50 fob Gulf on Thursday, its highest level since the Gulf War, on the back of sharp European demand and low stocks ahead of the northern hemisphere's winter.
"Europe has stoked this (Gulf) market...I doubt it will ease soon," a trader said.
A one percent sulphur cargo was sold at a $1 premium to fob Gulf price quotes, with limited remaining supplies finding eager homes in the Mediterranean and east Africa, traders said.
Gulf gas oil exports run at some 300,000 barrels per day.
Naphtha and fuel oil in the Gulf have also caught the fever from strong crude and Singapore product prices.

Fuel oil 380 cst grade, as well as bunkering supplies at Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates, have edged up to post-Gulf War highs and demand looks sufficient to keep prices within current ranges, traders said.
Jet kerosene markets look ready for further falls in outright and premium levels because of scant Far Eastern and Indian demand, traders said.
"The rally in outright prices is not encouraging the Chinese to buy...Prices will after to fall for buying to take off," one trader in the region said.
Jet kerosene was assessed at $28.80 -- still close to the year high of $31.85 in January -- with premiums talked between 30 cents and 40 cents.
Jet's premium to gas oil has shrunk from $2.75 a barrel in August to just 30 cents.
India Oil Corp (IOC) bought only one 0.25 percent sulphur superior kerosene cargo in its November delivery tender when the market had been expecting at least two to three cargoes.
Recent additional refining capacity in Thailand and South Korea was also trimming east of Suez requirements, particularly from Japan, for Gulf jet exports.
Term contract negotiations between Saudi Aramco and its term lifters for 1997 are continuing with no clear indication from Aramco of its pricing ideas, traders said.
Traders expect Aramco to secure higher premiums for term supplies.
Bahrain's Banoco on Thursday wrapped up some 1.5 million tonnes of gas oil and kerosene in term sales to IOC at premiums of around 70 cents and 50-55 cents.
